findings.title: AssignmentSource.queued is frozen at import time and not round-tripped as a datetime
findings.body: The `queued` field uses `timezone.now()` as a dataclass default, which Python evaluates once at module import, so every `AssignmentSource` constructed without an explicit value shares the process-start timestamp rather than recording when the source was queued. In addition, `from_dict` calls `cls(**input_dict)` directly, so when Celery's JSON serializer turns `queued` into an ISO string, the deserialized object has a `str` in a `datetime`-typed field and malformed values are silently accepted. This makes the field unusable for ordering/staleness/latency logic and breaks its declared type contract. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` and explicitly parse/validate `queued` in `from_dict`, or remove the field if it is not intended to be used.

findings.title: Core inbound and cross-integration suppression behavior is untested
findings.body: The only new test for cycle suppression calls `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` directly with a matching `AssignmentSource` and a single integration. It does not exercise the changed `sync_group_assignee_inbound` path that is supposed to attach the source from an inbound webhook, nor does it verify that a source from integration A still allows outbound sync to a different integration B. A regression where inbound forgets to pass the source, or where `should_sync` suppresses every non-`None` source, would still pass this suite even though the original loop would remain in production. Add tests that run `sync_group_assignee_inbound` with mocked outbound sync for both assign and deassign, plus a two-integration case proving that only the source integration is suppressed.
